title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.

progress.text: Backurs–Indyk prove a SETH-based obstruction to truly subquadratic exact edit distance; the 2017 full revision also records subsequent developments.
Bringmann–Künnemann establish the conditional lower bound already on binary strings.
A randomized approximation scheme obtains a quasi-polynomial speedup; it does not compute exact distances.

definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

sentences: Can exact edit distance between two length-n binary strings be computed in truly subquadratic time?
Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum.
The requested deterministic worst-case bound has a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n.
Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved.
The 2026 approximation improvement has different accuracy and randomness guarantees.
